questions.qtext: Which of the following are true about deadlocks? (choose all that apply):

options.text: Acquiring resources in a predetermined order is one way to avoid deadlock.
Rolling back threads is one way to address deadlock once it occurs.
Deadlock means that no threads are able to make progress.
Banker's algorithm is one way to recover from deadlock once it occurs.

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Correct Statements: A and B

Explanation:

  • A. Acquiring resources in a predetermined order is one way to avoid deadlock. (TRUE)

    • This is a classic Deadlock Prevention technique. By enforcing a global ordering on locks (e.g., always acquire Lock 1 before Lock 2), you make the "Circular Wait" condition structurally impossible. (Note: While strictly called "Prevention" in OS theory, "avoid" is often used colloquially in multiple-choice questions).

  • B. Rolling back threads is one way to address deadlock once it occurs. (TRUE)

    • This is a Deadlock Recovery technique. Once a deadlock is detected, the OS must break the cycle. It typically does this by preempting resources, killing a process, or rolling a victim process back to a safe checkpoint.

  • C. Deadlock means that no threads are able to make progress. (FALSE)

    • Deadlock only affects the specific set of threads involved in the circular dependency. Other independent threads in the system can continue to run normally.

  • D. Banker's algorithm is one way to recover from deadlock once it occurs. (FALSE)

    • The Banker's Algorithm is a Deadlock Avoidance technique used before allocation to prevent the system from entering an unsafe state. It is not used for recovery after the fact.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

  • Resource ordering breaks the Circular Wait condition, which prevents deadlocks from occurring.

  • Thread rollback restores a system to a saved checkpoint to recover from a deadlock that has already occurred.

  • Deadlock only blocks the specific threads waiting on those resources; un-involved threads can still make progress.

  • The Banker's Algorithm is a Deadlock Avoidance technique used before allocation, not a recovery mechanism.

Option A,B are correct

questions.qtext: Which of the following are true regarding Banker's Algorithm?

options.text: It only grants resource requests that will keep the system in a "safe" state so that it will have the potential to complete without deadlock.
It can always find an allocation of resources that avoids deadlock
If it detects an "unsafe" state, then the system is guaranteed to deadlock
It is capable of handling threads whose maximum possible resource consumption for a particular resource changes over time

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Correct Answer: A

Explanation:

  • A. It only grants resource requests that will keep the system in a "safe" state... (TRUE)

    • This is the core definition of the Banker's Algorithm. Before granting a request, it simulates the allocation. If the resulting state allows all processes to eventually complete (a safe sequence exists), the request is granted. Otherwise, it is denied or delayed.

  • B. It can always find an allocation... (FALSE)

    • If the system is already in an unsafe state or resources are exhausted, no valid allocation might exist.

  • C. If it detects an "unsafe" state, then the system is guaranteed to deadlock (FALSE)

    • An "Unsafe" state means there is no guarantee of safety (deadlock is possible). However, if processes don't actually request their maximum claim, a deadlock might not actually happen. Unsafe $\neq$ Deadlock.

  • D. It is capable of handling threads whose maximum... changes... (FALSE)

    • A major limitation of the Banker's Algorithm is that processes must declare their maximum resource needs in advance, and this number must remain fixed.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Banker's Algorithm is a deadlock avoidance method that checks if allocating resources keeps the system in a safe state, where every process can finish execution without causing a deadlock.

  • The algorithm only grants a request if a safe state is maintained, ensuring execution completes without deadlock.

  • However, if the system's total physical resources are simply insufficient to meet process demands, no safe sequence exists, meaning the algorithm cannot always find a resource allocation to prevent deadlock.

  • Being in an unsafe state does not guarantee a deadlock will occur, because processes may release resources early or never ask for their maximum claimed limit.

  • To make these safety calculations in advance, the algorithm strictly requires every thread's maximum resource consumption to be fixed and known upfront, making it incapable of handling maximum limits that change dynamically over time.

Option A is correct

questions.qtext:
Consider a system with three threads $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}$ and three mutex locks $x, y, z$. Each thread executes the following pseudo-code:
$$
\begin{array}{l@{\hspace{3em}} l@{\hspace{3em}} l}
\textbf{Thread } T_{1} & \textbf{Thread } T_{2} & \textbf{Thread } T_{3} \\\\
\text{acquire}(y) & \text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) \\
\text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) & \text{acquire}(y) \\
\text{release}(y) & \text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) \\
\text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) & \text{release}(y)
\end{array}
$$
All threads execute concurrently.

Which of the following sequences of lock acquisitions can lead to a deadlock?

options.text: $T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x})$
$T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z})$
$T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y})$

$T_{1}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{2}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}), T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y})$

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 1)
$$
\begin{aligned}
& T_{1}: \text { acquires } y \\
& T_{2}: \text { acquires } z \\
& T_{3}: \text { acquires } x \\
& T_{1}: \text { tries to acquire } z \text { (blocked) } \\
& T_{2}: \text { tries to acquire } x \text { (blocked) } \\
& T_{3}: \text { tries to acquire } y \text { (blocked) }
\end{aligned}
$$

This forms a circular wait:
$$
T_{1} \rightarrow y \rightarrow T_{3} \rightarrow x \rightarrow T_{2} \rightarrow z \rightarrow T_{1}
$$

Hence, deadlock occurs.
Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: We are looking for a sequence of execution steps that sets up a "Circular Wait".

  • T1 Needs: y,z

  • T2 Needs: z,x

  • T3 Needs: x,y

Analyzing Option B: T1​:acquire(y),T2​:acquire(z),T3​:acquire(x),T1​:acquire(z)

  1. T1​ acquires y. (T1 holds y).

  2. T2​ acquires z. (T2 holds z).

  3. T3​ acquires x. (T3 holds x).

    • At this point, every thread holds one resource and needs a second one held by its neighbor.

  4. T1​ attempts to acquire z.

    • z is held by T2​.

    • T1​ BLOCKS.

    • Now the system is locked:

      • T1​ waits for T2​ (z).

      • T2​ will wait for T3​ (x) (as soon as it runs).

      • T3​ will wait for T1​ (y) (as soon as it runs).

This sequence perfectly creates the deadlock cycle T1​→T2​→T3​→T1​.

(Note: Option A and C contain invalid instructions for T1. Option D is also a valid trace leading to deadlock, but Option B is the standard minimal answer showing the "Resource Exhaustion" followed by the "First Conflict".)

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Each thread must execute lock acquisitions in its exact specified code order: Thread T1 acquires y then z, Thread T2 acquires z then x, and Thread T3 acquires x then y.

  • Options A and C give invalid execution sequences that violate the pseudo-code, as T1 never acquires x and T1 must acquire y before z.

  • In sequence B, T1 acquires y, T2 acquires z, and T3 acquires x, putting all three primary locks in use before T1 attempts to acquire z (held by T2) and blocks.

  • Following T1 blocking in sequence B, T2's next code instruction is to acquire x (held by T3) and T3's next instruction is to acquire y (held by T1), causing all three threads to block and form a circular wait loop (T1 → T2 → T3 → T1).

  • In sequence D, T1 acquires y, T2 acquires z, and T3 acquires x, after which T2 requests x (held by T3) and T3 requests y (held by T1), blocking both threads.

  • When T1 then executes its next mandatory code step to acquire z (held by T2), T1 also blocks, creating the exact same circular wait dependency (T1 → T2 → T3 → T1) that leads to deadlock.

Option B,D are correct

Consider the same system with threads $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}$ defined as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{l@{\hspace{3em}} l@{\hspace{3em}} l}
\textbf{Thread } T_{1} & \textbf{Thread } T_{2} & \textbf{Thread } T_{3} \\\\
\text{acquire}(y) & \text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) \\
\text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) & \text{acquire}(y) \\
\text{release}(y) & \text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) \\
\text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) & \text{release}(y)
\end{array}
$$
The threads start simultaneously. Identify the point when the system first enters an $\textbf{unsafe state}$.

options.text: After $T_{1}$ acquires $y$
After $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}$ each acquire one distinct lock
After $T_{2}$ acquires $x$
After $T_{3}$ releases $x$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)
After:

$$
T_{1} \text { holds } y, \quad T_{2} \text { holds } z, \quad T_{3} \text { holds } x
$$

the system becomes unsafe any subsequent acquire() leads to circular wait and possible deadlock.
Source solution 2 (score: 0)

An unsafe state occurs when there is no safe execution sequence that allows all threads to acquire their required resources and finish execution without leading to a deadlock.

  • When only T1 acquires lock y, the other locks z and x remain free, so execution can still safely continue without any unavoidable dependency.

  • Once T1, T2, and T3 each acquire their first distinct lock (T1 gets y, T2 gets z, T3 gets x), all available locks in the system are held simultaneously.

  • At this exact moment, every thread requires a second lock that is currently held by another thread, making it impossible for any thread to complete without waiting on another, which forces the system into an unsafe state.

  • Options C and D occur after or during deadlock conditions and do not mark the initial point where the unsafe state is first entered.

Option B is correct

Consider the same system with threads $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}$ defined as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{l@{\hspace{3em}} l@{\hspace{3em}} l}
\textbf{Thread } T_{1} & \textbf{Thread } T_{2} & \textbf{Thread } T_{3} \\\\
\text{acquire}(y) & \text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) \\
\text{acquire}(z) & \text{acquire}(x) & \text{acquire}(y) \\
\text{release}(y) & \text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) \\
\text{release}(z) & \text{release}(x) & \text{release}(y)
\end{array}
$$
Initially, the program may experience deadlock due to circular waiting between these threads and $T_{3}$. To fix this, the student modifies $T_{3}$.
Which of the following implementations of $T_{3}$ will make the program deadlock-free regardless of the scheduler?

options.text: $T_{3} : \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}); \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}); \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{x}); \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{y})$
$T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}) ; \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{x}) ; \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{x}) ; \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{y})$
$T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(z) ; \operatorname{acquire}(x) ; \operatorname{release}(z) ; \operatorname{release}(x)$
$T_{3}: \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{y}) ; \operatorname{acquire}(\mathrm{z}) ; \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{z}) ; \operatorname{release}(\mathrm{y})$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)
$$
\text { Lock order: } T_{1}(y \rightarrow z), \quad T_{2}(z \rightarrow x), \quad T_{3}(y \rightarrow x)
$$

All threads now follow a $\textbf{consistent global ordering}$ among locks ( $y \rightarrow z \rightarrow x$ ), ensuring that circular wait cannot occur. Thus, the program becomes $\textbf{deadlock-free}$ under any scheduling scenario.
Source solution 2 (score: 1)

  • In Option A, Thread T3 tries to acquire x first and then y, keeping the same lock ordering as the original problem.

  • This allows Thread T1 to take y, Thread T2 to take z, and Thread T3 to take x simultaneously, creating a circular wait where T1 waits for z, T2 waits for x, and T3 waits for y, which causes a deadlock.

  • In Option B, Thread T3 is changed to acquire y first and then x, forcing both Thread T1 and Thread T3 to compete for lock y as their very first lock.

  • Whichever thread gets lock y first finishes execution while the other waits without holding any lock, completely breaking the circular wait and preventing deadlock under any scheduler.

  • Options C and D introduce lock z into Thread T3, but Thread T3 does not use lock z in the original pseudo-code, making them invalid sequence modifications.

So, Option B is correct

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Initially,

$$
T_1:\ acquire(y) \rightarrow acquire(z)
$$

$$
T_2:\ acquire(z) \rightarrow acquire(x)
$$

$$
T_3:\ acquire(x) \rightarrow acquire(y)
$$

From \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), the lock ordering already established is:

$$
y < z < x
$$

The original \(T_3\) acquires locks in the order:

$$
x \rightarrow y
$$

This creates a circular wait:

$$
y \rightarrow z \rightarrow x \rightarrow y
$$

Hence, deadlock is possible.

To make the system deadlock-free regardless of scheduler, all threads must follow a consistent global lock ordering.

Option A:

$$
x \rightarrow y
$$

Violates the established order. Hence, deadlock is still possible.

Option B:

$$
y \rightarrow x
$$

Consistent with the ordering:

$$
y < z < x
$$

The dependency graph becomes:

$$
y \rightarrow z,\quad z \rightarrow x,\quad y \rightarrow x
$$

No cycle exists, so deadlock is impossible.

Options C and D are not considered the intended answer because the question expects \(T_3\) to follow the prior implementation using x,y.

Hence, the correct answer is:

$$
\boxed{B}
$$

questions.qtext:
In a system, each lock is a $2$-mutex, meaning up to two threads can hold the same lock simultaneously.
A third thread attempting to acquire the same lock will block until one of the two holders releases it.
Consider two $2$-mutexes: $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, and three threads: $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}$, and $\mathbf{z}$.
The following sequence of lock acquisitions occurs:

  1. Thread $\mathbf{z}$ acquires $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$.
  2. Thread $\mathbf{x}$ acquires $\mathbf{a}$.
  3. Thread $\mathbf{y}$ acquires $\mathbf{b}$.
  4. Thread $\mathbf{x}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{b}$ (blocks).
  5. Thread $\mathbf{y}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{a}$ (blocks).

At this point, there is a cycle in the wait-for graph (edges from $x \rightarrow y$ and $y \rightarrow x$).
Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this situation?

options.text: The system is in deadlock, since a cycle always implies circular waiting.
The system is not in deadlock because $\mathbf{z}$ can release its locks and allow progress.
The system will remain blocked indefinitely, even if $\mathbf{z}$ releases its locks.
The scheduler must preempt $z$ to ensure progress of $x$ and $y$.

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 4)
Each lock is a 2-mutex, so two threads can hold the same lock simultaneously.

Here, $\mathbf{z}$ holds both $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, while $\mathbf{x}$ shares $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ shares $\mathbf{b}$.
When $\mathbf{x}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ tries to acquire $\mathbf{a}$, both block - forming a cycle in the wait-for graph.

However, this is not a deadlock, because $\mathbf{z}$ can still release both locks.
Once $\mathbf{z}$ releases them, $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ can proceed.

Hence, the system only experiences $\textbf{temporary waiting}$, not a true deadlock.
Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Each lock is a 2-mutex, meaning up to two threads can hold lock a and lock b simultaneously.

Thread z holds one unit of lock a and one unit of lock b, while thread x holds the second unit of lock a, and thread y holds the second unit of lock b.

Thread x gets blocked trying to acquire b because both units of b are taken (by z and y), and thread y gets blocked trying to acquire a because both units of a are taken (by z and x).

Now,

  • Although a cycle exists in the wait-for graph between x and y, the system is not in deadlock because thread z is not blocked by any resource and can continue execution.

  • Once thread z finishes its execution and releases its units of lock a and lock b, either thread x or thread y can acquire the freed lock and make progress.

  • Option A is incorrect because a cycle in a resource graph with multiple units per resource does not guarantee a deadlock.

  • Option C is incorrect because thread z releasing its locks unblocks x and y, allowing the system to make progress.

  • Option D is incorrect because thread z does not need to be preempted; it can finish its work naturally and release its locks.

Option B is correct

Consider a program with two threads \( T_1 \) (Pikachu) and \( T_2 \) (Mew), both using two mutex locks : \( \text{morph} \) and \( \text{levelup} \). The pseudo-code executed by each thread is shown below:

Thread \( T_1 \): Pikachu()
\[ \begin{aligned} &\text{lock}(\text{morph}) \\[3pt] &\text{lock}(\text{levelup}) \\[3pt] &\text{store some electricity} \\[3pt] &\text{unlock}(\text{levelup}) \\[3pt] &\text{unlock}(\text{morph}) \end{aligned} \]
Thread \( T_2 \): Mew()
\[ \begin{aligned} &\text{lock}(\text{levelup}) \\[3pt] &\text{lock}(\text{morph}) \\[3pt] &\text{become invisible} \\[3pt] &\text{unlock}(\text{levelup}) \\[3pt] &\text{unlock}(\text{morph}) \end{aligned} \]

Both threads start concurrently. Assume that mutex locks are standard and cannot be acquired again by the same thread before being released.


Which of the following statements is TRUE about the behavior of this program?

options.text: The program is deadlock-free because both threads eventually release all locks.
The program may deadlock if \( T_1 \) acquires <code>morph</code> and \( T_2 \) acquires <code>levelup</code> simultaneously, and preemption cannot resolve it.
The program may deadlock, but preemptive scheduling can break it by switching threads.
Deadlock cannot occur because both threads unlock all resources before exiting.

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Option A.The program is deadlock-free because both threads eventually release all locks.(False) because there is a possibility of deadlock if thread1 executes and preempts after acquring morph and thread 2 executes and preempts after acquring levelup

Option B.The program may deadlock if T1 acquires morph and T2 acquires levelup simultaneously, and preemption cannot resolve it.(True)

Option C.The program may deadlock, but preemptive scheduling can break it by switching threads.(False) because preemptive scheduling cannot break deadlock, and preemptive scheduling is the reason that may lead to deadlock

Option D.Deadlock cannot occur because both threads unlock all resources before exiting.(False)

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Deadlock occurs when thread $T_1$ acquires lock morph while thread $T_2$ simultaneously acquires lock levelup.

After these initial acquisitions, $T_1$ blocks waiting for levelup (held by $T_2$) and $T_2$ blocks waiting for morph (held by $T_1$), forming a circular wait.

Preemptive CPU scheduling only switches CPU execution time between threads, but it cannot forcefully revoke mutex locks held by a blocked thread.

  • Because preemptive context-switching cannot force a thread to release a mutex lock, CPU preemption cannot break or resolve the deadlock.

  • Options A and D are incorrect because releasing locks at the end of execution cannot happen if the threads are permanently blocked beforehand.

  • Option C is incorrect because preemptive scheduling merely rotates CPU time among blocked threads without releasing the locks needed to break the cycle.

Option B is correct

questions.qtext: Choose all methods that can help a system avoid or prevent deadlocks:

options.text: Allocate virtually "infinite" (i.e., a very large number of) resources that can be shared among threads.
Dynamically delay resource requests that would otherwise put the system in an unsafe state.
Request resources in a fixed order across all threads.
All of the above.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

  • Providing virtually infinite resources eliminates resource contention and competition, preventing threads from blocking each other and avoiding deadlock.

  • Dynamically delaying resource requests that would lead to an unsafe state is the core mechanism of deadlock avoidance algorithms (such as the Banker's Algorithm).

  • Requiring all threads to request resources in a strict, fixed global order eliminates circular waiting, which prevents deadlocks.

  • Since options A, B, and C are all valid strategies for avoiding or preventing deadlocks, option D is the correct overall choice.

Option D is correct

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

A. Allocate Virtually "Infinite" Resources

Allocate virtually "infinite" (i.e., a very large number of) resources that can be shared among threads: Deadlocks fundamentally occur due to contention over limited, mutually exclusive resources. If a system could theoretically provide virtually infinite or entirely shareable resources, threads would never have to wait for a resource to be freed, effectively preventing deadlocks by eliminating mutual exclusion.

B. Dynamically Delay Resource Requests

Dynamically delay resource requests that would otherwise put the system in an unsafe state: This is the exact definition of deadlock avoidance. Algorithms like the Banker's Algorithm operate by checking if granting a resource request will leave the system in a "safe state" (a state where all threads can eventually finish). If it leads to an unsafe state, the request is delayed.

C. Request Resources in a Fixed Order

Request resources in a fixed order across all threads: This is a standard deadlock prevention technique. By requiring all threads to request resources in a strict, predefined global order, you eliminate the possibility of a "circular wait" condition (e.g., Thread 1 holding A and waiting for B, while Thread 2 holds B and waits for A). Without circular wait, deadlocks cannot occur.

Answer: D

Source solution 3 (score: 0)
Answer : D. All of the aboveDetailed Breakdown:

  • A. Allocate virtually "infinite" resources that can be shared among threads: Deadlocks occur when threads compete for limited resources and must block waiting for others to release them. If resources are effectively unlimited, every request can be fulfilled immediately without blocking, eliminating resource contention and preventing deadlocks.

  • B. Dynamically delay resource requests that would otherwise put the system in an unsafe state: This is the precise definition of deadlock avoidance (most notably implemented via algorithms like the Banker's Algorithm). The system evaluates each allocation request to ensure it remains in a "safe state" where at least one execution sequence exists that allows all threads to complete.

  • C. Request resources in a fixed order across all threads: This is a classic deadlock prevention technique known as lock hierarchy / global resource ordering. Establishing a strict ordering invalidates the circular wait condition required for a deadlock to form.

questions.qtext: In the context of the Banker's Algorithm, which of the following best defines a $\textbf{SAFE state}$?

options.text: A state where all processes have been allocated their maximum required resources.
A state where no process is waiting for any resource at the moment.

A state where there exists at least one sequence in which all processes can complete execution without causing deadlock, without forcing any process to release resources prematurely, and while staying within their maximum declared needs.
A state that is not currently deadlocked but may lead to deadlock depending on future requests.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 0)
A SAFE state guarantees that there exists at least one deadlock-free sequence allowing every process to finish execution without violating their maximum resource requirements.
Source solution 2 (score: 0)

A safe state in the Banker's Algorithm guarantees that there is at least one execution sequence (a safe sequence) that allows every process to request up to its maximum declared need, finish running, and release its resources without encountering a deadlock.

  • Option A is incorrect because processes do not need to have all their maximum resources allocated at once; they just need to be able to request and receive them sequentially.

  • Option B is incorrect because processes can be in a waiting state while following a safe sequence as long as resources eventually free up to satisfy their requests.

  • Option D describes an unsafe state—a state that is not yet deadlocked but lacks a guaranteed safe sequence, meaning future requests could result in a deadlock.

Option C is correct

questions.qtext:
A system has $\mathbf{1 2}$ $\textbf{drives}$ in total.
Process A starts with $\mathbf{0}$ $\textbf{drives}$,
Process B starts with $\mathbf{4}$ $\textbf{drives}$.
Process A first requests $\mathbf{3} \textbf{drives}$, and then later requests $\mathbf{x}$ more drives, where $\mathbf{x>5}$ and $\mathbf{x} \leq \mathbf{9}$.
Process B may also randomly request more drives (if $\texttt{rand_bool()}$ returns true).
The system uses the \textbf{Banker's Algorithm} to avoid deadlock.
What will the Banker's Algorithm do when \textbf{Process A} makes its second request (for $\mathbf{x}$ drives)?

 
void process_A() {
 request_more_drives(3);
 request_more_drives(x); // where x > 5 and x <= 9
 free_all_drives();
}
void process_B() {
 if (rand_bool()) { // randomly true or false
 request_more_drives(i); // where 5 < i < 9
 }
 free_all_drives();
}

options.text: The first request in $\texttt{thread_A}$ (for $3$ drives) would be denied because it causes an unsafe state.
The second request in $\texttt{thread_A}$ (for $x$ drives) would be denied because granting it could lead to an unsafe state, even though the system might still run to completion without deadlock.
The system will always be safe regardless of the value of $\texttt{rand_bool()}$.
The system will immediately enter a deadlock after $\texttt{thread_B}$ calls $\texttt{free_all_drives()}$.

Answer: B

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

After the first call $\texttt{request_more_drives(3)}$,

  • $\textbf{Thread A}$ holds 3 drives,

  • $\textbf{Thread B}$ holds 4 drives,

  • $\textbf{Available $=12-(3+4)=5$}$.



So, the $\textbf{Banker's algorithm}$ denies A's second request - marking it as $\textbf{"unsafe"}$, even though in some runs (e.g., if $\texttt{rand_bool( )}$ is false and B doesn't request more) the system might still complete without deadlock.

$\textbf{Hence, the first request in A is safe, but the second one would be denied to prevent entering an unsafe state.}$

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

  • The system starts with 12 total drives: Process A initially holds 3 drives, and Process B holds 4 drives, leaving at most 5 drives free.

  • In the second request, Process A requests $x$ drives, where $x > 5$ ($x \in \{6, 7, 8, 9\}$).

  • Since the available drives (at most 5) are strictly less than the requested drives ($x \ge 6$), the system cannot safely grant this request.

  • The Banker's Algorithm denies or delays this second request to prevent the system from entering an unsafe state where deadlock could occur.

  • Option A is incorrect because the first request for 3 drives is safely granted from the available pool.

  • Option C is incorrect because if rand_bool() returns true, Process B's additional request creates competition that can make an uncontrolled state unsafe.

  • Option D is incorrect because calling free_all_drives() releases allocated resources back to the pool, which reduces resource pressure rather than causing a deadlock.

for option b,

  • Since $x$ is strictly greater than 5 ($x \in \{6, 7, 8, 9\}$), Process A requests at least 6 drives.

  • Granting this request would require more drives than the system currently has available (at most 5 drives left), or it would leave remaining drives insufficient to satisfy Process B's potential maximum need ($i$ drives, where $5 < i < 9$).

Option B is correct

A system has $\mathbf{3}$ threads ( $\mathrm{T} 1, \mathrm{~T} 2, \mathrm{~T} 3$ ) and $\mathbf{3}$ resource types ( $\mathrm{R} 1, \mathrm{R} 2, \mathrm{R} 3$ ). The current state of the system is given as:
$$\textbf{Available}: (R 1, R 2, R 3)=(0,2,1)$$
$$
\begin{array}{c}
\textbf{Allocations} \\
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\textbf{Thread} & R1 & R2 & R3 \\
\hline
T1 & 1 & 2 & 2 \\
T2 & 5 & 0 & 1 \\
T3 & 10 & 3 & 6 \\
\end{array}
\end{array}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{array}{c}
\textbf{Requests} \\
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\textbf{Thread} & R1 & R2 & R3 \\
\hline
T1 & 3 & 0 & 2 \\
T2 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\
T3 & 1 & 3 & 3 \\
\end{array}
\end{array}
$$
Each thread can run only if its request $\leq$ currently available resources. Once a thread completes, it releases all its allocated resources back to the system.
Which of the following represents a valid order of thread execution that allows all requests to be satisfied without deadlock?

options.text: $T 1 \rightarrow T 3 \rightarrow T 2$
$T 2 \rightarrow T 1 \rightarrow T 3$
$T 3 \rightarrow T 2 \rightarrow T 1$
$T 1 \rightarrow T 2 \rightarrow T 3$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Initially, Available $=(0,2,1)$.

  • Run T2: Request $=(0,1,1) \leq(0,2,1) ightarrow$ allowed.

After completion, T 2 releases $(5,0,1)$.
New Available = (5,2,2).

  • Run T1: Request $=(3,0,2) \leq(5,2,2) ightarrow$ allowed.

After completion, T 1 releases $(1,2,2)$.
New Available $=(6,4,4)$.

  • Run T3: Request $=(1,3,3) \leq(6,4,4) ightarrow$ allowed.

After completion, T3 releases ( $10,3,6$ ).
Final Available $=(16,7,10)$.


All threads complete successfully with no deadlock. Hence, the system is safe with the sequence:
$$
oxed{T 2 ightarrow T 1 ightarrow T 3}
$$

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

  • Initial Available resources are $(R1, R2, R3) = (0, 2, 1)$.

  • Comparing current Available $(0, 2, 1)$ against each thread's Request matrix:

    • $T1 ext{ Request} = (3, 0, 2) ot\le (0, 2, 1)$ (Needs 3 of $R1$ and 2 of $R3$, but 0 and 1 are available).

    • $T2 ext{ Request} = (0, 1, 1) \le (0, 2, 1)$ (Can execute!).

    • $T3 ext{ Request} = (1, 3, 3) ot\le (0, 2, 1)$ (Needs $R1$ and more $R2, R3$).

  • Only thread $T2$ can run first. Once $T2$ completes, it releases its allocation $(5, 0, 1)$ back to the system, updating Available to $(0, 2, 1) + (5, 0, 1) = (5, 2, 2)$.

  • With new Available $(5, 2, 2)$:

    • $T1 ext{ Request} = (3, 0, 2) \le (5, 2, 2)$ (Can now execute!).

    • $T3 ext{ Request} = (1, 3, 3) ot\le (5, 2, 2)$ (Needs 3 of $R2$ and $R3$, but only 2 are available).

  • Thread $T1$ runs next and releases its allocation $(1, 2, 2)$, updating Available to $(5, 2, 2) + (1, 2, 2) = (6, 4, 4)$.

  • Finally, with Available $(6, 4, 4)$, thread $T3$'s request $(1, 3, 3) \le (6, 4, 4)$ can be satisfied, giving the execution order $T2 ightarrow T1 ightarrow T3$.

Option B is correct

questions.qtext:
Suppose physical memory can store $\mathbf{N}$ pages, and our demand paging system uses an LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement policy. If a process's resident set contains ( $\mathbf{N + 1}$ ) distinct pages that are accessed sequentially forever, i.e.,
$$
P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N}, P_{N+1}, P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots
$$
what will be the hit rate of this demand paging system?

options.text: The hit rate tends to $\frac{1}{N+1}$
The hit rate tends to $\frac{N}{N+1}$
The hit rate is $0$
The hit rate is $1$

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 3)
Since the process accesses $N+1$ pages sequentially and memory can hold only $N$ pages, each time a new page is referenced, it will evict the least recently used page which happens to be the one needed next. Thus, every access results in a page fault and no hits occur.

Example sequence:
$$
\text { Access } P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{N} \text { fills memory. }
$$

Next access $P_{N+1}$ evicts $P_{1}$. Then accessing $P_{1}$ evicts $P_{2}$, and so on. Hence, every reference causes a fault.
$$
\boxed{\text { Hit rate }=0}
$$
Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Correct Answer: C. The hit rate is 0

Explanation: This scenario describes the worst-case behavior for the Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement algorithm. This phenomenon is often colloquially referred to as "looping over a working set that is just slightly too large."

Step-by-Step Simulation: Let's verify this with a small example.

  • Assume Memory Size N=3.

  • Sequence size is N+1=4 distinct pages: 1,2,3,4.

  • Access pattern: 1,2,3,4,1,2,3,4,…

1. Filling Memory (Cold Start):

  • Access 1: Miss. Memory: [1] (LRU: 1)

  • Access 2: Miss. Memory: [1, 2] (LRU: 1)

  • Access 3: Miss. Memory: [1, 2, 3] (LRU: 1)

  • Memory is now full.

2. The First Eviction:

  • Access 4: Miss.

    • LRU policy evicts the least recently used page, which is 1.

    • Memory becomes: [2, 3, 4] (LRU: 2).

3. The Loop Begins (The Problem):

  • Access 1: Miss. (Page 1 was just evicted in the previous step!)

    • LRU policy evicts the current LRU page, which is 2.

    • Memory becomes: [3, 4, 1] (LRU: 3).

  • Access 2: Miss. (Page 2 was just evicted!)

    • LRU policy evicts 3.

    • Memory becomes: [4, 1, 2] (LRU: 4).

Conclusion: In this specific scenario where the loop size (N+1) is strictly larger than the cache size (N), the page needed for the next access is always the exact page that was identified as "least recently used" and evicted during the previous miss.

Therefore, every single memory access results in a page fault, and the hit rate is exactly 0.

Source solution 3 (score: 1)

The memory has $N$ page frames, and the process accesses $N+1$ distinct pages sequentially in a loop: $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_N, P_{N+1}, P_1, P_2, \dots$

Under LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement policy, when page $P_{N+1}$ is requested, memory is full with $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_N$.

  • Since $P_1$ was accessed furthest in the past, LRU evicts $P_1$ to bring in $P_{N+1}$.

  • The next requested page is $P_1$, which was just evicted, so it causes a page fault and LRU evicts $P_2$ to bring $P_1$ back.

  • This pattern repeats continuously for every single page access in the sequence, causing a page fault every single time ( known as thrashing).

  • Since every single access results in a page fault (miss), the number of hits is 0, making the Hit Rate = 0.

Option C is correct
